newsitem.title: FRANCE: Carlos the Jackal struggles to have book banned.
newsitem.headline: Carlos the Jackal struggles to have book banned.

text.p: Jailed guerrilla "Carlos the Jackal" battled on Tuesday to have a book about him banned on the grounds that it violated his right to be presumed innocent.

Lawyers for Venezuelan-born Carlos and the publisher of "Carlos: The Secret Networks of International Terrorism" locked horns at a hearing in the Paris law courts. Carlos, who has been in a Paris jail since August 1994, was not present.

The presiding judge heard the guerrilla's criticisms of the book by French journalist Bernard Violet and decreed a pause to give Seuil, the publishers, time to prepare a reaction to the detailed accusations.
She said parties would reconvene later on Tuesday, but justice sources said she was likely to delay a decision for a week on whether to ban the book.
"What I object to is the mercenary motivation, the desire to get rich on the back of my client," said lawyer Frederic Pariente, representing Carlos
"This book, published without the knowledge of my client, is dishonest and violates the rights of the defence, notably the presumption of innocence."

Pariente denounced the use of Carlos's picture on the front cover of the book, 8,000 copies of which have been printed. He demanded 350,000 francs ($70,000) as an advance payment in damages for what he termed an attack on Carlos's image and on his right to be presumed innocent.

Carlos, whose real name is Illich Ramirez Sanchez, formally objected to "the revelation of facts which pertain to his private life" -- including references to his school record, an affair with a Cuban student and to a testicle operation in Sudan shortly before he was seized and spirited to France in 1994.

Pariente said distribution of the book should halted and existing copies seized. Failing that, a statement inside each copy should clarify that Carlos's "participation in the events mentioned has never been established".
A spokeswoman for Seuil said on Monday that the cover on the photograph had already been published elsewhere. She had no comment on the other allegations.
The book draws on questioning of Carlos by Paris anti-terrorism judge Jean-Louis Bruguiere, files of the former East Germany's Stasi secret services and other material.

Before he was detained in Sudan, Carlos had been sentenced to life in prison in his absence for shooting dead two French secret service agents in Paris in 1975. Later in 1975 he led the kidnapping of 11 OPEC oil ministers from a conference in Vienna.
French prosecutors accuse him of killing 83 people in a series of attacks mostly in Europe and the Middle East and he is under investigation for four other bombings in France in the 1980s.
